title: Do you really think AAA is actually happy about the "democratization" of game dev?
author: Frosty-Cockroach-807
selftext:
Tim Sweeny, CEO of Epic Games, has become an X warrior pushing for the acceptance of AI in game dev.

The thing is, no AAA company would be happy about a technology that threatens their business model.

So why is Sweeny championing the "democratization" of game dev? Because he realizes that the more hobbyists flood the market with low-effort AI games, the harder it will be for indie studios or solo devs to actually gain visibility and survive.

The indie scene will be drowned out by the flood, and AAA, with their massive marketing budgets, will clamp down further on the gaming industry. In the end we'll be left with AAA slop or hobbyist slop.

Let Steam, GOG, and other game publishing companies figure out how to filter away the slop. There's plenty of slop on YouTube but yet, I see very little of it. It's there but it mostly gets filtered away from my feed. Easy enough for Steam to greenlight all the big AAA studios from those filters.

comments.author: heavy-minium
comments.body:
Just a little bit, maybe, but not massively threatened.  
Things where the gap between AAA studios and indie gets smaller and smaller over time: Voice acting, Motion capture, Video content, reproducing a real environment, Story writing, Concept art and similar. Those were the things that used to be hard to get for an indie studio. But then again, they can do it cheaper now too, so their budget can get smaller or they can achieve more with the same budget.

But they still have an edge in a few things, which are for example playtesting, market data and analysis, infrastructure, distribution pipelines, IP rights, Community management, VFX, etc... and most importantly, marketing, which indies suck at.

So it's not like this is a death sentence for AAA. But it's definitely closing a lot of gaps.

What's also likely to happen is that AAA will find a way to work around the recent ease of reverse engineering games or stealing ideas - online live services, game streaming, more DRM stuff, patents, hordes of lawyers, etc... Meanwhile indies will have very little sway in dealing with that.

comments.author: Total_Engineering_51
comments.body: Unreal Engine and Fortnite are platforms for people to build games on, and he is seeing the writing on the wall with AI opening doors for game dev that were previously closed… meaning that people are going to build stuff with AI regardless of the current gatekeepers desires. That leaves two choices for Epic(and Unity and Roblox), either open things up for this new wave or go full turtle and hope they can keep market share until the “fad” ends. It’s obvious he would rather embrace that movement and see people stay on Epic’s platforms instead of having them slowly go somewhere else. The EGS side is secondary and is just him taking the opportunity to poke at Valve and their somewhat regressive and generally inactive handling of AI so far. Compared to Unreal Engine and Fortnite, EGS is basically a rounding error in terms of Epic’s revenue.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
>Tim Sweeny, CEO of Epic Games, has become an X warrior pushing for the acceptance of AI in game dev.

>The thing is, no AAA company would be happy about a technology that threatens their monopoly over the industry.

  
...I am not some big authority on the industry, but I have engaged with it and do know it: 

I think people would be surprised at how much 'fck it, we ball' energy is in the AAA companies people like to shit on. No, there is not some moustache-twirling villain CEO sitting in their office, hellbent on ruining games forever. Game studios are more like R&D firms than product manufacturing firms; there's a lot of risk, a lot of experimentation, and so if you're going to be an effective leader in that business, you have to be able to accept that the house is always going to be at least a little bit on fire  

. A game industry CEO that didn't migrate here from another industry is here for the love of the game. Like, they have to be. This is the worst industry to be a CEO in - you're hated AND you make no money, mostly 

  
I suspect that while motivations here are a mixed bag, Sweeney is genuine in his enthusiasm and optimism. He wants to see wild and crazy shit people make with the new tools. Seeing wild and crazy shit get made is why he participates in the industry

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
>So why is Sweeny championing the "democratization" of game dev? Because he realizes that the more hobbyists flood the market with low-effort AI games, the harder it will be for indie studios or solo devs to actually gain visibility and survive.

>The indie scene will be drowned out by the flood, and AAA, with their massive marketing budgets, will clamp down further on the gaming industry. In the end we'll be left with AAA slop or hobbyist slop.

>AI will never make a AAA or even AA game, and if it ever reaches that point, the ladder will get pulled up faster than you can say "make no mistakes, claude".

  
So, to be clear, this hyper-cynical take is the only possible reason Sweeney could be interested in the technology? He, what, goes to work every day cackling about how he is going to kill games for everyone and stomp on the indy games scene that... his friends, co-workers and family members likely all participate in? Because he's such a BAD GUY, yeah! 

And then when he gets to the office, he probably kicks a puppy they've got chained up next to the door just so Sweeney can kick it every day! 

  
I love how platforms have encouraged the deepening and the spread of this kind of outlook on the world. 

  
Could it be that there are nuanced, overlapping and pretty normal reasons for someone like Sweeney to think that AI tools are an important part of the future, pivot to their adoption and encourage other people to do the same? No, no no no - it must be part of his evil 4D chess master plan to DESTROY independent game development with SLOP!
